courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: How a stale CAS corrupts a lock-free stack
md: CAS checks *equality of value*, not *absence of change*. Any algorithm that reads a pointer, computes from what it points to, and then CASes on that pointer is wrong if the pointed-to node can be recycled in between.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Add-one-in measures a stage in isolation; leave-one-out measures its marginal value in the system you will ship. When the two disagree, the stages interact, and that disagreement is itself a finding worth reporting.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Case: First American Financial and 885 million documents (2019)
md: First American had two failures. The code failure was a missing object-level check. The process failure was treating a confirmed exposure of hundreds of millions of sensitive documents as low severity. Severity comes from what the bug exposes, not from how simple the bug is.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
md: Authorization is tested by asking the wrong user. For every endpoint, decide in advance what anonymous users, other users, other tenants and admins should get, write it down as a matrix, and make the build fail when reality differs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline
md: Kerberoasting works because any user may request any service ticket and the ticket is locked with a key derived from the service account's password. Remove human passwords from service accounts (gMSA), drop RC4, keep them unprivileged, and alert on RC4 4769s for user-owned SPNs.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: When the DC itself has the bug: Zerologon, noPac, PrintNightmare
md: DC bugs turn a foothold into the domain in minutes, so DCs are patched first and fastest, run no extra services, and go to enforcement mode early. Zerologon, noPac and PrintNightmare each have specific events to watch.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Case: Follina (CVE-2022-30190), a document with no macro
md: Patches end a bug; detections outlive it. Word starting msdt.exe was abnormal before May 2022 and is still abnormal now, so the behaviour rule keeps catching the next abuse of a protocol handler.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Never use one keystream twice. Reusing keystream material across files turns any file whose original you hold into a key for others. Sound designs encrypt each file with its own key from a proper cipher and protect the master secret with public-key encryption.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Exploit chains: renderer bug, sandbox escape, kernel bug
md: A full compromise of a hardened platform is a chain, usually renderer RCE plus sandbox escape plus kernel bug. Each extra wall forces another 0-day, and each stage is a separate chance to detect or break the attack.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Running a purple team exercise
md: A purple team exercise is a loop per technique: context, expectation, execution, investigation, fix, retest, record. The output is not a list of what the red team achieved but a list of what the blue team can now see that it could not see in the morning.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
md: Resolved means: the patch applies, and **every** FAIL_TO_PASS test and **every** PASS_TO_PASS test is found and passes. Fixing the issue while breaking one old test scores exactly the same as doing nothing.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
md: Treat tool design like UI design for a new colleague: clear names, documented parameters, concise high-signal output, guardrails that turn likely mistakes into instructive errors. Changing the tool often beats changing the prompt.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Verification turns "the agent says it is done" into "independent evidence says it is done". How much you can trust a shipped result is bounded by how often the verifier passes wrong results.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
md: Treat the environment as part of the training algorithm. Its reward defines what is learned, its isolation defines what can be cheated, and its throughput (containers times 3600 divided by episode seconds) defines how many steps you can afford.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The lethal trifecta and excessive agency
md: "Read-only" tools are not harmless in a trifecta. A tool that only fetches URLs is a perfect exit: the data goes out in the request.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: MCP and agent tools: when tool descriptions are the attack
md: Every MCP server you add is code you run and text your model obeys. Install few, from publishers you trust; pin and review their descriptions; show full arguments on approval; sandbox local servers; and do not combine private-data tools, untrusted-content tools and outbound tools in one agent.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: Materials generators are diffusion models over a mixed object (types, periodic coordinates, lattice). They change where candidates come from; MLIPs and DFT still decide which are stable, and novelty must be checked against experimental databases.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
md: What interposition misses: statically linked programs (LD_PRELOAD is a feature of the dynamic linker), secure-execution binaries such as set-user-ID programs (the linker ignores LD_PRELOAD paths with slashes), and any memory that bypasses malloc: direct mmap, custom arenas and pools, GPU allocations. heaptrack's README notes pool allocators need code annotations to be profiled.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: LOF answers a different question from Isolation Forest: not how isolated a point is, but how isolated it is relative to its own neighborhood. Use it when normal data has regions of very different density; pay for it with k-nearest-neighbor searches and a k to tune.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), item by item
md: Most of the API Top 10 is not exotic. It is a missing check (who owns this, who may call this, how many times), a forgotten endpoint, or misplaced trust in another system.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OpenID Connect: logging users in with an ID token
md: ID token: for the client, proves a login happened (check aud = your client_id and nonce). Access token: for the API, grants access (the API checks aud = itself). Never accept one where the other is expected.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to API and token attacks
md: Tokens move the security perimeter into data: who issued it, with which key, for which audience, for how long. Log those fields on every request, alert on the impossible ones, and rehearse revoking at scale.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Writing rules: Semgrep and CodeQL on the same code
md: Write a custom rule when a bug teaches you a pattern: after every incident or review finding, ask "where else does this pattern appear?" and encode it. That is variant analysis, and it turns one fix into a class fix.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SSVC: decisions instead of scores
md: SSVC turns "how bad is it?" into "what do we do, and how fast?". The inputs that matter most are exploitation status and your own context: exposure and how essential the system is. A score cannot know the second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: ARIES in one line: **repeat history, then undo the losers, logging every undo as a redo-only CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips what is already undone**. That makes recovery **idempotent**, meaning that running it again after a partial run ends in the same state as running it once: crash during analysis or redo and you simply start over; crash during undo and you resume where the CLRs say.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: `gather` does not cancel siblings on failure. With the default `return_exceptions=False`, the first exception propagates to the caller but the docs state the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". If you want per-item errors without losing the batch, pass `return_exceptions=True` and inspect each result; if one failure should stop everything, use a `TaskGroup`.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: The budget only helps tasks that keep awaiting **Tokio** resources. It cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop or a blocking call, and the Tokio team has said it will not detect blocked workers and add threads automatically. Fixing those is your job.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: A pretrained audio model never sees a whole clip at once. It sees fixed 0.96 s log-mel patches and returns one embedding and one score vector per patch. Everything about clip-level decisions (lesson 3) is about combining those per-patch outputs.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: How offline cracking works: guesses, lists, rules and arithmetic
md: Offline cracking = guess, hash, compare, at the attacker's full hardware speed. Defenders control two things: how many guesses a password needs (length, unpredictability, blocklists) and how expensive each guess is (a slow, salted hash).

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Wearing MFA down: SIM swaps, push fatigue and Uber 2022
md: MFA is only as strong as its weakest step. SMS inherits the phone network's weaknesses; plain push inherits human fatigue. Number matching helps against fatigue; phishing-resistant MFA removes the whole class.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: x86-64 on Linux and macOS: the System V calling convention
md: Do not apply Windows habits to Linux binaries. On Windows the first argument is in `rcx`; on Linux and macOS `rcx` is the fourth. Misreading the convention shifts every argument by several positions and makes a correct analysis look nonsensical. Check the file format first: PE means Microsoft x64, ELF or Mach-O on x86-64 means System V.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
md: "1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: Predictors learn *regularity*: biased branches, periodic patterns, and (next lesson) correlations with other branches. A branch on random data with a 50/50 split is mispredicted about half the time on every CPU, no matter how clever the predictor.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Bloom filters only help point lookups. A range scan must open every run that overlaps the range and merge them, so the RocksDB guide counts scan read amplification as (L0 files) + (non-empty levels). Tiered layouts with many runs pay most for scans.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers
md: Real systems combine a cheap recency approximation with a second signal: PostgreSQL uses counts plus per-operation rings, InnoDB uses a two-segment list with a time threshold, and 2Q and LRU-2 use a remembered first reference. The common goal: a page must prove reuse before it can displace the hot set.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: High availability is not disaster recovery: GitLab, January 2017
md: High availability copies every change, good or bad, as fast as it can; it protects against component failure. Disaster recovery needs copies that did *not* follow the bad change: point-in-time backups or snapshots, kept separately. Ask of every copy: which failures does it survive?

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When the building burns: OVHcloud 2021 and DR site strategies
md: A disaster recovery copy must sit outside the failure domain of the disaster: another building is not enough if the site is isolated, another zone is not enough if the control plane deletes both. Pick a site or cloud strategy by RTO and cost, and fail over with the most available mechanisms.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Common misconception: byte models are slow because attention is quadratic. Efficient attention (methods and kernels such as FlashAttention that make attention cheaper or faster) helps small models, but the BLT authors point out that at scale the cost is dominated by the large feed-forward layers that run on **every** position. Fewer positions through the big network is what matters.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Limitations the authors list: their FLOP matching is theoretical and the implementation may not yet match token models in wall-clock time; the entropy model is trained separately rather than end to end; and they borrowed BPE scaling-law data ratios that may not be optimal for BLT. BPE still won word deletion and word insertion on CUTE.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
md: `unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: A common misconception is that memory cost is proportional to the bytes your code reads. It is proportional to the **lines it touches**. Reading 8 bytes from each of 1,000 scattered lines moves 64,000 bytes through the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
md: Collapsing chains is not free. If the real model really runs a mutually reinforcing loop (the paper sees Copenhagen and Denmark features exciting each other with per-layer transcoders), a CLT can hide it. Simpler graphs can mean less faithful graphs.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Lab: trace, label and intervene on a real graph with circuit-tracer
md: Graph, then labels, then interventions, then a report that names its own gaps. The graph proposes; only the measured change in the real model, including the swaps that fail, counts as evidence.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: XSS: when your page runs someone else's code
md: An `HttpOnly` session cookie does not make XSS harmless. It stops script from *reading* the cookie, so the attacker cannot take the session home. But the injected script does not need the cookie value: it sends requests from the victim's own browser, and the browser attaches the cookie for it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
md: Prevention lives in code (encode, sanitise, safe sinks, tokens, allowlists). Detection lives mostly in the browser (CSP and Trusted Types reports) and in monitoring of what your pages load. A team that only watches server logs is blind to DOM XSS and skimmers.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Reading CloudTrail like a responder: who really made this call?
md: Misconception: "the event names the role, so the role's owner did it". A role is a costume many identities can put on. Attribution needs the chain: issued key to used key, back to a long-term credential, a federated sign-in or a workload.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Uber 2022: from one contractor's login to the cloud consoles
md: Misconception: "the CloudTrail logs show no data access, so the cloud was not affected". If an attacker held a vault administrator account, every stored credential must be treated as exposed. Absence of use in the logs you have narrows the impact; it does not remove the need to rotate.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Graphing attack paths: role chains, PMapper and Access Analyzer
md: Least privilege is a property of the graph, not of one policy. Ask "who can reach this role or this data, through any chain?", fix the cheapest edge on each path, and rerun the analysis after every IAM change.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy
md: IAM starts from deny. A request is allowed only if some applicable policy explicitly allows it and no applicable policy explicitly denies it. Write policies as a list of what is needed, never as a list of what to forbid.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Catching misconfigurations early: infrastructure as code and CSPM
md: Scanners produce a lot of findings, and most teams drown in them. Rank by what an attacker could do: public exposure of sensitive data, wildcard IAM on roles reachable from the internet, IMDSv1 on internet-facing instances and disabled logging come before "detailed monitoring is off". A posture tool is only as good as the triage behind it.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Five criteria on the same ten points: the elbow is ambiguous, VRC says k = 5, silhouette says k = 3, BIC with a variance floor says k = 3, and the gap statistic says one cluster. That disagreement is the lesson. Schubert's advice is to use a baseline-aware criterion (VRC, BIC or the gap statistic) rather than an elbow, and to spend your effort on preprocessing, "because garbage in, garbage out".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: From tuple-at-a-time to vector-at-a-time execution
md: Vectorization keeps the iterator model but changes its unit from one tuple to a cache-sized vector. That amortizes interpretation overhead (small n is bad) without materializing whole columns in RAM (huge n is bad).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO, -march and fast-math can each beat any -O level, but each adds a condition: representative profiles, a known target CPU, and numerics that tolerate reordering.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Assume the model will sometimes be wrong or hijacked, and design so that it does not matter much: isolate the machine, keep secrets and broad network access out of it, require a human for irreversible actions, and check every action before it runs.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: Use loom to search **schedules** of a tiny test exhaustively, and TSan to check **ordering** on real runs of the whole program. Neither proves correctness alone; together they cover far more than any number of stress runs.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
md: W + R greater than N guarantees that a read sees every *completed* write. Linearizability also needs reads to agree with each other while a write is in flight. ABD gets that by making each read finish only after its result sits on a quorum.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
md: A `should` clause is not an OR filter when the query also has a `filter` or `must` clause, because minimum_should_match then defaults to 0. Putting a hard requirement in `should` silently turns it into a mere preference. Set `minimum_should_match` explicitly if you need at least one of several options to match.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: Common mistakes. **CP-SAT works over integers only**: a coefficient like 0.5 must be scaled (multiply the constraint by 2). A status of `FEASIBLE` after a time limit is not a proof of optimality, and `UNKNOWN` is not a proof of infeasibility. With more than one worker, runs are not guaranteed to be repeatable; tests and demos often set `num_workers = 1`.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
md: privileged, extra capabilities, hostPath, runtime sockets, hostPID and hostNetwork each turn a container back into a process on the host. If a workload asks for one, ask why, and isolate it if the answer is real.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
md: Misconception: "we enforce Restricted, so pods are safe". PSA checks pod fields only. It does not check the image, RBAC, network policy or which Secrets are mounted, and namespaces or users can be exempted in its configuration. It is one layer.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
md: Misconception: "we have audit logging, so we would see an attack". The audit log sees API requests. An attacker who never calls the API server (kubelet exec, a runtime escape, a miner in an existing pod) leaves no audit events. Pair it with node-level runtime detection and network flow logs.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Model the state as a fixed schema where every slot is present and null means unconstrained. Each turn applies one of a few explicit operations per slot, and carryover is the default.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Misconception: "if every step of the CoT is correct, the CoT explains the answer." Turpin et al. found unfaithful CoTs with no obvious errors. Checking that reasoning is *valid* tests plausibility. Only a counterfactual (change an input the CoT ignores and see if the answer moves) tests faithfulness.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
md: Three independent facts, often confused. A stream gives you **ordering** (and is always sequential inside itself). Separate streams give you **permission** to overlap. The hardware (`asyncEngineCount`, concurrent kernel support, free SMs) decides whether overlap actually **happens**. Two streams on a one-copy-engine GPU will still serialize their two transfers against each other.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
md: Hard negative mining has a trap: MS MARCO labels about one relevant passage per query, so many top-ranked unlabeled passages are actually relevant. Training to push them down teaches the model wrong lessons. mine_hard_negatives offers margins and a max_score cap partly to skip such false negatives.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision
md: "It is only a checksum" is how MD5 and SHA-1 linger. Any place where an attacker can choose the input that gets hashed (certificates, signed documents, deduplication, commit ids, package lockfiles) needs collision resistance.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Padding oracles: when an error message decrypts your data
md: A padding oracle needs two things: decryption of unauthenticated ciphertext, and any observable difference (message, status code, timing, log line, connection reset) between padding failures and other failures. Remove the first and the second cannot matter: authenticate before you decrypt.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Never trust parameters: invalid curves, blank signatures, pinning
md: "The library checks that" is a claim to test, not assume. Java's verifier was a mainstream library. Run published test vectors such as Project Wycheproof against the exact library versions you ship.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
md: Atoms are hardware facts, TiledMMA and TiledCopy are spatial arrangements of atoms, and partition_A/B/C or partition_S/D (source and destination) turn a tile into per-thread fragments. Swapping the atom (FMA, mma.sync, wgmma) changes the instruction without rewriting the loops.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Do not assume every CXL device behaves like Pond's model. Sun et al. measured three real devices: one had load latency only 35% longer than a remote-socket DDR5 node, while the other two were about 2x and 3x longer. Their bandwidth efficiency also differed widely by controller. Emulating CXL with a remote NUMA socket, as early research did, can mislead in both directions.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: Van Buren is not a licence. Misusing data you may open can still be fraud, a privacy violation, a breach of contract, a firing offence or a state crime (lesson 4). And it says nothing about getting past a gate that is down: guessing a password or exploiting a bug to reach an area is still the off-limits kind.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Writing and selling tools: Marcus Hutchins and dual-use code
md: Writing security tools is legal almost everywhere. Laws target tools designed primarily for crime and people who supply them intending, or believing likely, criminal use. Context is evidence: who you sell to, how you advertise, what the features are for.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Evidence in court: authenticity, hearsay and chain of custody
md: Courts ask: is it what you say it is (authenticity), was it made routinely at the time (business records), and who could have changed it (chain of custody)? Automatic logs, hashes at collection and a tamper-evident custody record answer all three.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Using 280M-proxy weights for an 8B model is an empirical bet that good weights transfer across a 30x jump in scale. It paid off here, but the paper lists why weights transfer, and how far, as open questions, and its 1B proxy produced a worse 8B model than the 280M one (lesson 6). Weights also assume a token budget: lesson 5 shows what happens when you reuse them for a longer run.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Cleaning the crawl: heuristic rules, perplexity filters, exact dedup
md: Clean before you mix. Cheap rules remove describable junk, a perplexity filter keeps text resembling a reference (with its biases), and exact plus near deduplication removes copies. Each step shrinks domains, so redo the epoch math of lesson 5 and rerun the mixing step on the cleaned data.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
md: List the hot loops, write down which fields each one touches and whether it streams or jumps, then pick the layout that packs those bytes together. Re-measure when the access pattern changes.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Tokens and masks: taking real values out of systems
md: Dynamic masking changes what is displayed, not what can be queried. Against anyone who can write their own WHERE clauses it is not a security boundary; use column permissions (lesson 8), tokens or encryption there.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a data security programme, and practice
md: Data security is a loop: find, label, keep less, protect, watch, destroy, with each finding feeding back into the inventory. Measure each stage, and judge controls by who can still cause the data to be read.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Replaying failures, the limits of DST, and who uses it
md: DST turns rare, timing-dependent bugs into seeds. The engineering cost is up front (every source of nondeterminism behind an interface, plus good oracles), and the return is that every bug found is a bug you can replay and fix.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a secure pipeline, a response plan, practice
md: The question to ask of every part of a pipeline: who can change what this runs, and what can it reach when it does? If the answer to the first is "anyone who can open a PR" and to the second is "production", there is a gap, however many scanners run.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Do not read 'parallel generation' as 'all tokens in one step'. Quality drops quickly when many interdependent tokens are committed together; useful systems unmask a few to a few dozen tokens per pass depending on confidence.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: The registry in depth, and proving a USB drive was used
md: A VSN changes when a volume is reformatted and is only 32 bits on FAT, so a match is strong corroboration, not a unique fingerprint. Combine it with the device serial and times. The meanings of the 0x64 to 0x67 properties also vary by Windows build: test on a reference system before testifying to them.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Vamana: RobustPrune and the alpha knob
md: A common misreading: larger alpha prunes *more*. It is the opposite. The removal test gets harder to pass as alpha grows, so more candidates survive, the average degree rises (up to the cap R), and search paths get shorter. The cost is memory and more distance computations per hop.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: KTO keeps DPO's implicit reward and reference model but drops pairing: each example is scored against a shared reference point (the estimated KL drift) instead of against a sibling answer. That lets it train on binary feedback, and on imbalanced data via $\lambda_D, \lambda_U$.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
md: The verifier runs once, at load time, and proves properties of **all** paths: bounded execution, typed pointers, null checks before dereference, initialized registers, in-bounds stack and map access. Because the proof is done up front, the JIT-compiled code needs no runtime checks and runs at native speed.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Edge devices: the doors attackers now try first
md: An edge appliance combines the three things attackers want most: anyone can talk to it before logging in, it holds credentials with reach inside, and it is usually the least observed computer you own.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Management interfaces: keep the admin door off the internet
md: The service may need the internet; the admin interface does not. Put management on its own network or behind a separate enforcement point, and prove it with an outside scan.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss
md: Response length growth during RL is partly an optimizer artifact. Check the loss normalization (a constant normalizer as in Dr. GRPO, $\lambda < 1$ for PPO) and the mix of solvable problems before adding a length penalty, and log length separately for correct and incorrect rollouts.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
md: The modes are far apart on hard problems. Qwen3-235B-A22B scored 85.7 on AIME 2024 thinking and 40.1 without. Fusion also had a price: for Qwen3-32B, thinking-mode AIME 2024 fell from 83.8 to 81.4 after the fusion and general-RL stages. A user-chosen switch is only as good as the user's guess about difficulty.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
md: Microsoft states AppLocker is "a defense-in-depth security feature and not considered a defensible Windows security feature": it does not meet Microsoft's servicing criteria, so a bypass is not treated as a vulnerability. Use it to raise the bar and to control what users run; use App Control for Business where you need a security boundary.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
md: Event-based methods need step changes. Hart's own NALM page lists three appliance classes: ON/OFF (bulbs, toasters), multi-state (washing machines, dishwashers with fill, rinse and spin states) and continuously variable (light dimmers, variable-speed tools). The last class is hard to monitor nonintrusively because it does not generate step changes in power.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs: whether pairs scored 0.9 really match about 90% of the time.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: Count who can become Global Administrator, not only who is one: role assigners, admin credential resetters, app credential managers and hybrid identity admins. Keep the count small, make it eligible rather than active, and keep two tested emergency accounts outside it.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Entra access is a chain: a 60 to 90 minute access token renewed by a 90-day refresh token that is bound to user and client, not to a resource. Revocation cuts the chain; CAE cuts the current link at Exchange, SharePoint, Teams and Graph.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: A Conditional Access policy set is only as strong as what it does not cover. Inventory the exclusions, the service principals and the allowed flows, block legacy authentication and device code, and test every change in report-only mode first.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: Common misconception: "the binary has every mitigation enabled, so this overflow is not a security issue." Every mitigation in this course has a known bypass class (lesson 14), and real exploits combine several bugs to get past them. An overflow is a security bug whether or not today's exploit techniques reach it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer (a race detector such as ThreadSanitizer, which flags conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory) to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
md: On our toy problem, a proximal term with $\mu = 2$ moves the $E = 5$ fixed point from 1.944 to 1.995 and slows the first round from 1.320 to 0.988. It buys accuracy with speed, and it does not reach 2.3. Treat these methods as damping on drift, not as a cure; the honest cure for this toy is $E = 1$ or a control-variate correction.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
md: Sampling cost is set by how curved the learned paths are. A perfectly straight, constant-speed flow is solved exactly by one Euler step.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
md: Writing the invariant as `idx < n` looks natural but is wrong twice. Verus reports "invariant not satisfied before loop" (n can be 0) and "invariant not satisfied at end of loop body" (the last iteration makes idx == n).

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: The scale is a full-precision real number kept outside the FP8 data (in FP32), not a change to the format's exponent bias. The FP8 paper chose this deliberately: a software scale can take any value, while a programmable bias could only shift by powers of two.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Calling fsync on a file does not necessarily make the file's **directory entry** durable. A newly created or renamed file also needs an fsync on a file descriptor for the directory, or after a crash the name may be missing.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
md: A harness plus a sanitizer turns 'run the parser on generated bytes' into an automatic bug finder: coverage guidance reaches deep code, comparison tracing gets past magic values, and ASan converts silent corruption into a report with a saved reproducer.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
md: Stateful targets need stateful fuzzing: keep a valid prefix, mutate later messages, use responses or coverage to recognise new states, and reset the target between sequences. Firmware that skips basic mitigations (no stack cookies) makes every such bug worse.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities (parity here means whether the image is mirrored or not). Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context: the driver's per-process state on the GPU, such as loaded kernel code and the driver's own buffers, which uses device memory that PyTorch's counters never include. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: The graph is an LLM's *abstractive summary* of the corpus (written in the model's own words, not copied sentences), not a parse of it. Every node and edge carries an LLM-written description, and those descriptions, not the raw text, are what later stages summarize.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: Verifiable does not mean perfect. A verifier can reject correct answers (12.0 versus 12) or accept wrong ones (a unit-test suite that misses edge cases). Real pipelines normalize answers; for example, Tulu 3's 'flex' MATH evaluation tries three different ways to extract the final answer, because models often ignore the requested format. The quality of the checker caps the quality of the signal.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
md: Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.0 and client-side desync: when a server ignores the body
md: Every code path must leave the connection in a known state: either it consumed exactly the declared body, or it closes the connection. Cache hits, redirects, errors and static files are the paths that forget.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: Huge pages pay off three ways: one TLB entry covers 512 (or 262,144) times more memory, each miss walks fewer levels, and the page tables shrink. The kernel's THP doc calls the fourth effect, one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512, almost irrelevant because it only happens on first touch.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
md: RRF is not parameter-free. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (TOIS 2023, ACM Transactions on Information Systems) gave each retriever its own k and showed that nDCG swings noticeably when those constants are changed, and that constants tuned in-domain did not transfer reliably out of domain. Also, the window size is a hidden parameter: a document at rank 11 with a window of 10 contributes nothing at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
md: Changing a setpoint and changing the program are different. Setpoints are data the program reads (often over the network, by design, from the HMI). The program is the logic itself. Both can steer the process; defenders must watch and protect both.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
md: It is tempting to read 2015 as 'malware turned off the lights'. Investigators found BlackEnergy but could not show it played a role in the outage; people turned off the lights, through legitimate remote access. Monitoring that only looks for malware would have missed it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Misconception: SSO means one session. It means one *login*. After it, the IdP has a session and every app has its own, with its own cookie and lifetime. Disabling a user at the IdP does not end the app sessions already issued (lesson 10).

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Sessions across apps: IdP session, app sessions and logout
md: Offboarding gap: disabling a user at the IdP stops new logins, not existing app sessions or refresh tokens. A complete offboarding or account-takeover response also ends sessions in each app: through back-channel logout or signals where supported, through the app's admin API or SCIM deactivation (next lesson) where not.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: A common misconception is that identity and access management means single sign-on. Single sign-on proves who is logging in, once. It says nothing about whether Ana should still hold payroll access three jobs later. Governance works on the access itself, over time.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Just-in-time admin and break-glass accounts
md: A break-glass account that nobody monitors is just a permanent, policy-exempt Global Administrator. Its safety comes entirely from being rare, strongly authenticated, loudly alerted and regularly tested.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
md: RFC 3227 names programs to avoid on a live suspect system, such as `tar` or `xcopy`, because they update the access time of every file they touch, overwriting evidence of what the attacker read.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
md: Clocks start at awareness or determination, not at the end of the investigation. If you wait until you know everything, you will be late. Plan for phased notices: first what you know, then updates.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
md: Patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. After an injection that may have been exploited, look for persistence (web shells, new accounts, changed configuration) and for what data left, using web, database and network logs.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: eval, new Function and why node:vm is not a sandbox
md: Inside one process, JavaScript objects are a graph, and any shared object is a path back to the host. node:vm, vm2 and similar tools are useful for running *your own* code in a clean global, never for running someone else's. Untrusted code needs a process, container or VM boundary.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
md: Without `background_thread`, purging runs inside your application threads as they call into jemalloc, which adds to their tail latency, and an inactive application delays purging. jemalloc's tuning guide suggests `background_thread:true` where extra jemalloc-managed threads are acceptable.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle is sound but not complete: everything it reports is real, but it can miss anomalies. A cycle found is real, yet missing cycles prove nothing: appends never observed by a later read leave gaps in the version order, and predicate anomalies (like phantoms, rows matching a WHERE clause that appear or vanish between two reads in one transaction) are outside its analysis.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Misconception: bypass is mainly about avoiding copies. The kernel already offers zero-copy paths. At 14.88 Mpps the killers are fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, mode switches, metadata setup, shared locks), which is why minimum-size packets are the benchmark that matters.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Treat distillation as function matching: same input to teacher and student every step, as many distinct inputs as you can generate, and a schedule far longer than supervised training. Judge the run against a same-size model trained on labels, and track agreement with the teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
md: HLC is still one-way like Lamport: $(l, c)$ ordering never tells you two events are concurrent. Its gain is closeness to real time and constant size, not concurrency detection.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: ColBERT and ColPali are the same idea at different granularities: keep one vector per token or patch, precompute the document side, and let each query token pick its best match.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Coconut reached 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4. The probes suggest deferring commitment is part of why, but staged training without any thoughts also reached 95.5%.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: An RMI separates model size from execution cost. A lookup evaluates exactly one model per stage, however many leaf models exist. Adding leaves makes each leaf's slice smaller and its error bounds tighter without adding work per lookup.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is one function with two schedules: a **parallel form** $O=(QK^\top\odot M)V$ that is matmul-friendly for training, and a **recurrent form** $S_t=S_{t-1}+v_tk_t^\top$, $o_t=S_tq_t$ with constant time and memory per generated token.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: What a fixed state cannot do: recall limits and state tracking
md: Do not mix the two limits up. A bigger state helps recall but does nothing for parity: with eigenvalues in [0, 1], even a huge state fails at long lengths. Negative eigenvalues fix parity but add no storage. Production models answer the recall limit by keeping some attention layers (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in
md: A cron job run by root that executes a script writable by another user is a privilege escalation waiting to happen: whoever can edit the script chooses what root runs every night. When auditing, check the permissions of every file a root job calls, not only the crontab line.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise
md: Patch, expose less, use keys, grant little, keep logs off the box and keep baselines. Each step is simple; together they turn most of the attacks in this course from silent root into a noisy, short-lived event.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Kernel lockdown modes and sysctl baselines across a fleet
md: Use lockdown integrity mode on fleets that run eBPF or kprobe sensors; confidentiality also blocks the reads those sensors need. Lockdown only ever goes up until reboot. For sysctl, the last-sorted file wins across directories, so always verify running values, not config files.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: A kprobe policy depends on a kernel function name and its arguments, which are not a stable interface and can change between kernel versions. Test policies against every kernel version in your fleet, and watch for the policy failing to load after a kernel update.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: regreSSHion across a fleet, from advisory to verified fix
md: Fleet response = package-aware inventory, immediate exposure reduction through config management, ring rollout with restarts, verification of running code, and detection of the attack's noise in the meantime. Never triage on upstream version strings alone.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
md: Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
md: Masking the model's input and output does not mask everything else. The AWS docs say Bedrock invocation logs (its record of each model call) keep the original request, and the `match` field of the guardrail trace (the per-request report of what each policy found) contains the original PII value by design. Protect logs and traces separately.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Fixed-size blocks plus a per-request table make KV memory behave like virtual memory: allocate on demand, any block fits anywhere, and waste is bounded by one partial block per sequence.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: From regex to JSON Schema: grammars, stacks and real engines
md: The constraint and the prompt are separate channels. A mask can stop the model from writing an illegal token, but it cannot tell the model what the fields mean. If the model never sees the schema (as with llama.cpp's grammar option), describe the fields in the prompt, or the model is forced through a format it does not understand.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
md: Design for the miss: the parse cache sets the mean, the deadline and keyword fallback set the tail.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Do not compare quality numbers across papers as if the setups matched. First-stage retrievers, candidate depth and datasets differ (RankGPT and PRP rerank BM25 top 100; FIRST reranks Contriever top 100). Re-measure on one pipeline.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris scores a window by how much it changes under shifts in every direction. Both eigenvalues of $M$ large means corner; that is what makes a point localizable in two dimensions.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
md: The log you need is usually older than the moment you learn you need it. Decide what to collect and how long to keep it from the questions an investigation will ask, then pay for that deliberately.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Alert quality: precision, recall and the base-rate trap
md: Low precision does not just waste time; it trains people to ignore alerts. Target's alerts were real, but an alert stream that is usually wrong teaches analysts that the next one probably is too. Precision is a security property.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches
md: Per-token early exit saves FLOPs per token, but in batched serving tokens that exit early may sit idle waiting for others. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al. 2024) propose **continuous depth-wise batching**, scheduling new work into slots freed by early exits; their simulation estimates 2 to 3x throughput, not a measured deployment.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model
md: QLoRA separates a storage type (NF4, 4 bits) from a compute type (BF16). Only the adapters are trained, so quantization error in the frozen base can be compensated by the adapters, and memory drops by about 4x versus a 16-bit base.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Reading x86-64 assembly: registers and core instructions
md: You do not need to read every instruction. Analysts skim for calls (what API is used?), compares and conditional jumps (what decision is made?), and constants (what string, size or key is used?).

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Indicators of compromise and the Pyramid of Pain
md: Hashes and IPs are for fast, cheap blocking and for searching history. Artifacts, tools and TTPs are what keep working next month. Report both, but build your detections near the top of the pyramid.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
md: Every axis splits something different: TP splits matrices, PP splits layers, DP splits the batch, CP splits the sequence, EP splits experts. Choosing a configuration means choosing which communication you can afford on which link.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Virtual addresses, page tables and the DTB, walked by hand
md: If an entry's present bit is 0, the page is not in RAM: it may be in the page file, compressed, or never used. The data is then simply not in a raw image. Tools report such reads as invalid addresses or blank fields, and an absent value is not evidence that something did not exist.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Linux memory: banners, task lists, bash history and kernel checks
md: Linux images fail more often than Windows ones because of symbols. Before an incident, build or collect ISF files for the kernels you run (the volatility3-symbols project publishes some pre-generated ones), and record `uname -a` at collection so you know which banner to match. The `-u` (`--remote-isf-url`) option lets Volatility search an online ISF index; `--offline` stops all downloads.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: "Fragmentation is solved" is not the lesson. The study covers eight single-threaded C and C++ programs from the 1990s, and the authors call for more work on unusual program behaviour. Long-running servers with phase changes, many threads and per-thread caches are exactly that kind of workload, as the next lesson shows.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: `volatile` is not an ordering. In standard C++, volatile accesses are not atomic and do not order other memory, so they cannot be used for synchronization between threads. (MSVC, Microsoft's C++ compiler, gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads (more runnable threads than cores, so some are always preempted), update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
md: Every allocation size and every length passed to memcpy should come from a computation that cannot overflow and a value that cannot be negative. When a size comes from a file or a packet, validate it against the real data first.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS (a video-based re-ID dataset) in their supplementary material.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Repeat, interleave, and report the mean with a confidence interval (or a median with its spread). Never decide from one run or from the best of N.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
md: TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
md: Misconception: "we never exported that activity, so it is not exported." Libraries add components to the merged manifest at build time. Review the manifest of the APK you ship (lesson 3), not the one in your repository.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: Cache size per token is set by what you store per token per layer. MQA and GQA shrink it by sharing keys and values across heads. MLA's bet is different: store one small learned vector per token and let each head derive its own keys and values from it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: Union and RRF are not interchangeable. A union returns everything (N x k documents at worst) in retrieval order, so taking its first k usually just returns the first query's list. Pick RRF when the next stage has a fixed budget; pick union when a reranker will score all candidates anyway.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
md: **Distillation** turns an expensive stage into a teacher for a cheaper one. Run the slow model offline on training queries, then train a fast model to imitate its rankings. You pay the teacher's cost once, at training time, instead of on every query.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
md: A frequent mistake is to read $L^{-1/4}$ as an elementwise power. It is a *matrix* power: eigendecompose $L = Q \Lambda Q^\top$ and take $Q \Lambda^{-1/4} Q^\top$. That needs float32 (or better) and an eigensolver, which is why roots are only refreshed every $f$ steps.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon in a real training stack: parameter groups, sharding and code
md: Give Muon the hidden 2D matrices (Q, K, V kept separate), AdamW everything else. In PyTorch that is two optimizers stepped together. Distributed, Muon costs one extra bf16 gather per matrix and every rank's Newton-Schulz on the full matrix, against one fewer state buffer than AdamW.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why 'maximal': kernel, mean-field and feature-learning limits
md: Every stable parametrization is, at large width, either a kernel machine with frozen features or a feature learner. muP is the feature learner in which every layer moves as much as stability allows: that is what "maximal update" means.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What muP does not transfer: horizon, weight decay, the SP debate
md: muP transfers across width; depth needs a branch rule; the token horizon needs an LR correction (about $D^{-0.32}$ at large scale); weight decay needs its $\eta\lambda$ timescale held fixed; regularization needs retuning.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: Choosing a lock: in application code use the standard mutex, which is already uncontended-fast and spin-then-sleep. Reach for a pure spin lock only where the holder cannot be preempted and sections are tiny, as in a kernel with preemption disabled. Reduce contention itself (shorter sections, or sharding: splitting the data into parts that each have their own lock) before tuning spin counts.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI has **false positives**. Not every dangerous structure is part of a real cycle, so some aborted transactions would have been fine. The paper reports serialization failure rates well under 1% on its benchmarks and an overall cost under 7% versus plain snapshot isolation, but your workload may differ.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
md: When labels are scarce, spend them on **measurement** first and **training** second. A few hundred carefully labelled lines plus a pile of noisily labelled ones beats a thousand rushed labels with no held-out set, because without a trustworthy eval you cannot tell whether any change helped.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
